summary:
Consensual sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the Penal Code, in force since 2018, sets an equal age of consent regardless of sex, while keeping heavier penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Legality is not the same as protection: the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and no criminal ruling on the same-sex provisions had ever been rendered as of Benin's statement to the 2008 review, on the government's account because families would not allow children to be brought to court.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and there is no protection on grounds of gender identity at all. Legal gender recognition is impossible. A trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection to invoke.

The protections that do exist are narrow and mostly concern data and speech. Article 394 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code prohibits processing personal data that reveals sex life or sexual orientation; Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law bars collection or processing without express consent; Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts based on sex or real or perceived sexuality. Article 552 of the same 2017 Digital Code punishes provoking discrimination, hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation through an electronic communications network or computer system with one year's imprisonment and a five million franc fine, or one penalty only, in force since 2018.

Benin does not recognise LGBTQI+ couples or families. The one sourced exception is the grant of diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children's Code, Law 2015-08, bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption.

Healthcare access is the sharpest practical exposure. Providers regularly refuse treatment related to LGBTQ status, including gender-affirming hormone therapy, and also refuse general care such as malaria treatment. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, with transgender and intersex people singled out.

Violence against LGBTQI+ people is documented as common, particularly outside major urban areas, and includes arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment. Anti-gay lynchings are described as commonplace and are mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities; police rarely pursue perpetrators. The sources give no count of killings and no general homicide rate for Benin, so no comparison between trans-specific and background violence can be made here.

Reporting is suppressed. People who report violence or discrimination to police conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity for fear of mistreatment, and lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely report at all.

Religious institutions are a significant source of hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries and priests are documented calling transgender people demons. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques take part in homophobic preaching, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy, often coerced by families.

State responses have been limited. Benin rejected recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons at the 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that "certain things would be rectified". At the 2023 Universal Periodic Review the government accepted two of fifteen recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV.

Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions on LGBT people.

No source in the inventory records tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatisation; the transgender-specific material is limited to the "demons" preaching and to hiring discrimination that names transgender and intersex people.
tangentialFactors:
Benin's current statute sits against a longer legislative record. Article 331 of the old Penal Code, as amended in 1947, punished an indecent act or act against nature with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 200 to 50,000 francs. Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent act or act against nature with an individual of the same sex with one to three years' imprisonment and a 100,000 to 500,000 franc fine, but was never voted into law. The October 2008 draft contains no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and has not been voted on.

Regional religious hostility is documented across Benin's neighbourhood. A 2015 account commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups records LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describing discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. The piece is dated 2015 and is context rather than current-state evidence.

Public attitudes frame homosexuality as unnatural and as an import from outside the region, with homosexuals treated as deviants and homosexuality often described as a disease brought by white people.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register in Benin. Against that, the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has run a 20-place temporary accommodation centre for LGBT+ youth since about 2020, through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed.

Family rejection is common and drives the shelter need. LGBTQ people are frequently rejected by their families and have difficulty getting jobs. The government provides sexual and reproductive healthcare for people who have experienced sexual violence, but LGBTQ people are typically denied medical care and social services.

Public events are possible. On 17 May 2013 LGBTQ associations in Cotonou organised an International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at the Institut Français that drew 200 people, and organisations are able to hold public events.

The statutory legality rests on older practice rather than recent liberalisation. An interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo cites evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom, the territory of modern Benin.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace is not accompanied in the inventory by a count of killings, a date range or a general homicide rate for Benin, so its magnitude cannot be assessed and no trans-specific rate can be stated.

The 2015 Washington Blade account is a decade old and is treated as context, not as evidence of the current situation.

The shelter figures appear in two forms in the sources: a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people have passed since about 2020, and 20 shelters housing 380 LGBTQ people between 2020 and 2024. Which figure is accurate is unresolved.

Whether the general indecency provision is currently used to prosecute same-sex conduct is not dated in the sources. The statement that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered on the same-sex provisions dates from Benin's submission to the 2008 review.

The 2013 note that "certain things would be rectified" is not tied to any enacted measure. Implementation of the two recommendations accepted at the 2023 Universal Periodic Review is not sourced.

Several findings, among them conversion therapy by imams, priests and traditional healers, separate Catholic cemeteries, and the refusal of gender-affirming hormone therapy, rest on a single encyclopaedic source in the inventory and are not corroborated by the other sources listed.
